item.title: Beattie hails new era for Fiji rugby league
item.description: Australian Rugby League Commission commissioner Peter Beattie has described the new 10-year partnership with Fiji National Rugby League as a landmark moment for the development of rugby league in Fiji. item.content:encoded:
Australian Rugby League Commission commissioner Peter Beattie has described the new 10-year partnership with Fiji National Rugby League as a landmark moment for the development of rugby league in Fiji.

Speaking during a press conference today at the FNRL Office, Beattie said the agreement, witnessed by the Prime Minister, would focus on growing the game from the grassroots while creating opportunities for young Fijians to develop through rugby league.

“This is the most significant day for rugby league in the history of Fiji,” Beattie said.

He said the partnership was about more than producing players for the NRL, with the wider objective of encouraging boys and girls to participate in sport and develop important life skills. Beattie said rugby league could play an important role in keeping young people active and engaged while helping them build discipline, teamwork and resilience.

The 10-year plan will focus on implementation across schools and communities, with coach development, infrastructure and player pathways identified as key areas.

Beattie said schools would be a major priority, with programmes expected to introduce children to rugby league from a young age.

He stressed that the partnership was not simply designed to create a pathway for players to leave Fiji and pursue careers in Australia.

While some talented players could progress to the NRL, Beattie said the priority was to strengthen rugby league within Fiji and give young people the opportunity to play and develop at home.

“This is about building capacity here,” he said.

Women’s rugby league will also form an important part of the programme, with Beattie highlighting the need for more opportunities for girls and women to participate and develop their skills.

He said investment would include coach education, player development and pathways, as well as improved tackling techniques to promote player safety.

The partnership will also support the Fiji National Rugby League in strengthening its ability to track registrations and monitor player development.

Beattie said having accurate participation data would allow the sport to understand who was playing, follow their progress and provide appropriate support as they moved through the pathways.

Player welfare will also be a key consideration, particularly in relation to concussion.

Beattie said the ARLC would work with the Fiji National Rugby League to ensure players were properly monitored and given sufficient time to recover before returning to competition.

Accountability will also be built into the partnership, with systems to ensure funding is properly managed and directed towards the agreed programmes.

Beattie said the groundwork had already been completed through consultation and planning, with the signing now allowing the implementation phase to begin.

The partnership is expected to strengthen rugby league at school, community and provincial levels while creating a more structured development pathway for future generations.

For Beattie, the long-term vision is clear, build a stronger rugby league system in Fiji while giving young Fijians the opportunity to benefit from the sport, whether or not they ultimately reach the NRL.

item.title: Deans: From North to the national rugby stage
item.description: Ravulo believes Kanawabu has returned from the national age-grade environment with valuable knowledge that has benefited the entire Navatu squad. “He has shared his knowledge and experience with his fellow Northern brothers on what he went through in the rugby pathway,” Ravulo said.
item.content:encoded:
Ravulo believes Kanawabu has returned from the national age-grade environment with valuable knowledge that has benefited the entire Navatu squad.

“He has shared his knowledge and experience with his fellow Northern brothers on what he went through in the rugby pathway,” Ravulo said.

“It has really boosted the team and inspired many to follow in his footsteps.”

For Ravulo, Kanawabu’s journey carries a message beyond Navatu.

It shows young players from the North that despite the challenges and limited opportunities they may face, they can still break into Fiji’s national age-grade teams.

Kanawabu, meanwhile, remains grateful for the opportunity to return to the Northern schools rugby scene with Navatu and be part of a team that has rewritten the school’s history.

“I am grateful for the opportunity coach Ravulo gave me to play at Navatu Secondary School,” Kanawabu said.

“It has enabled me to be part of the historic rise of the school in the competition.”

Now the captain has one final challenge this season.

Navatu faces Lelean Memorial School in the Vodafone Super Deans U19 final at the HFC Bank National Stadium in Suva this Saturday.

Kanawabu said the team must remain grounded despite reaching a historic final.

“We will remain humble and work on our mistakes from the semi-final,” he said.

“We will come back with the same attitude and mindset against Lelean.”

After the Super Deans, Kanawabu hopes to return to his island team, Taveuni, for the Skipper Cup campaign.

Beyond that lies an even bigger ambition — to make a career out of rugby.

For now, however, his focus is on Navatu and the final.

From Holy Cross College to Bucalevu, from the Fiji Schoolboys U18 team to Navatu, Kanawabu’s journey has already taken him a long way.

item.title: U19: Lelean survives tough test
item.description: LELEAN Memorial School assistant principal Ulaiyasi Vakatawakoula praised his players for holding their nerve after they defeated Ratu Navula College 36-27 in a thrilling U19 semi-final at Churchill Park on Saturday. Vakatawakoula thanked Ratu Navula for pushing his side throughout the match and said the team would now turn its attention to the final.
item.content:encoded:
LELEAN Memorial School assistant principal Ulaiyasi Vakatawakoula praised his players for holding their nerve after they defeated Ratu Navula College 36-27 in a thrilling U19 semi-final at Churchill Park on Saturday.

Vakatawakoula thanked Ratu Navula for pushing his side throughout the match and said the team would now turn its attention to the final.

“We thank Ratu Navula for giving us a very tough game right to the final whistle. We are thankful to the boys and we are very humble with the win.

“We will go back now and prepare for the final. We will look at our mistakes and try to work on them and improve for the final, ” he said.

Lelean’s victory secured its place in the U19 final, where it will have an opportunity to claim the title.

Meanwhile, Ratu Navula College also secured a place in the U14 final after edging Ratu Kadavulevu School 26-25.

Ratu Navula will face Queen Victoria School in the U14 final.

item.title: Lomary’s rise to Raluve final
item.description: LOMARY Secondary School has turned a stunning semi-final performance into a place in the Weetbix Raluve under-18 final, defeating Sila Central College 24-10 in a powerful display of determination at the HFC Bank National Stadium in Suva on Saturday. With the biggest prize of their campaign within reach, the Lomary girls rose to the occasion when it mattered most, producing the performance that has
item.content:encoded:
LOMARY Secondary School has turned a stunning semi-final performance into a place in the Weetbix Raluve under-18 final, defeating Sila Central College 24-10 in a powerful display of determination at the HFC Bank National Stadium in Suva on Saturday.

With the biggest prize of their campaign within reach, the Lomary girls rose to the occasion when it mattered most, producing the performance that has carried them one step away from championship glory.

The 24-10 victory was more than just a win. It was a statement from a team that has grown together throughout the competition and now finds itself on the biggest stage of the Raluve U18 championship.

Captain Ema Leba Gade admitted the occasion was overwhelming, but said her team remained composed enough to deliver.

“It was so loud and overwhelming. We played so good, but I would say that we will go back and work on our weaknesses and come back in the finals and have a good play time,” Gade said.

For Lomary, however, there is little time to celebrate.

The captain said the team was ready for whatever challenge awaits in the final.

“We are looking forward to any team that we will play against in the finals.”

Gade believes the foundation for their breakthrough run was laid through hard preparation and the unity within the squad.

“The preparation was hard, I could say, because we came in and won our semi-finals. We have achieved a very good result,” she said.

She reserved special praise for her teammates, whose togetherness has become one of Lomary’s greatest strengths.

“I am so grateful for the girls that stick together, work together and the bond of the team that we have achieved.”

Next week Saturday, Lomary stands 70 minutes away from history. Standing in their way in the final will be Mahatma Gandhi Memorial School, setting the stage for a mouth-watering showdown between two teams with the Raluve U18 crown firmly in their sights.

For Lomary, Saturday’s victory was the breakthrough.

The final is where they must finish the job.

item.title: Nand: Winning goal for sister
item.description: IXCEL Rewa FC forward Merril Nand dedicated his crucial goal to his elder sister after helping Rewa secure a place in the semi-finals of the OFC Men’s Champions League on Wednesday. Rewa entered their final pool match against Lae City knowing it was a must-win encounter if they were to keep their semi-final hopes alive.
item.content:encoded:
IXCEL Rewa FC forward Merril Nand dedicated his crucial goal to his elder sister after helping Rewa secure a place in the semi-finals of the OFC Men’s Champions League on Wednesday.

Rewa entered their final pool match against Lae City knowing it was a must-win encounter if they were to keep their semi-final hopes alive.

Lae City scored first in the opening half, but Nand said the Rewa players remained confident they could fight their way back into the match.

“We went into our last pool match knowing it was a must-win for us for us to make it to the semi-final.

“We talked about it in camp, the importance of this match, and we came back stronger in the second half after Lae City scored the first goal in the first half.

“The boys believed that we would get the win,” Nand said.

Nand then delivered when it mattered most, scoring the crucial goal to help Rewa secure the victory and book their place in the last four.

He credited God for giving him the strength to score and thanked the team management for believing in him.

“I thank God for giving me the strength to score that goal and I thank the team management for believing in me,” he said.

Nand dedicated the goal to his elder sister, who is serving as a tournament doctor and is also preparing for her wedding.

“I dedicate it to my elder sister who is actually a tournament doctor and is getting married.”

With Rewa now preparing for the semi-final, Nand has called on their supporters to turn out in numbers.

“To the fans, come out in numbers for the semi-final. I hope more fans come out in numbers and support us,” he said.

Rewa coach and player Tevita Waranivalu praised the players for their determination and effort in securing their semi-final berth.

“I am happy with the boys. They fought hard and they wanted to be in the semi-final.

“I reminded them that it would not be an easy match, but we had to fight hard to be in the semi-final,” Waranivalu said.

Waranivalu said he urged the players at halftime to remain composed and stick to their game plan.

“In the second half, I told the boys to stick to the game plan. I want to thank God for always being on our side from day one,” he added.

Rewa now has three days to prepare for the semi-final, with Waranivalu saying the team’s immediate focus will be on recovery and assessing injuries.

item.content:encoded:
From the village of Lavena on Taveuni to the biggest stage of Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby, Vilimone Kanawabu’s journey has been shaped by opportunity, hard work and the guidance of a coach who believed in him early.

Now, the Navatu Secondary School under-19 captain and number eight stands on the brink of making more history as his team prepares for the U19 final in the Vodafone Super Deans this Saturday.

Kanawabu joined Navatu Secondary School this year after spending last season at Bucalevu Secondary School.

Prior to Bucalevu, he attended Holy Cross College, with each stage adding another layer to his rugby development.

Last year, while at Bucalevu, Kanawabu earned selection in the Fiji Schoolboys U18 team, an experience that has now become an important part of his leadership at Navatu.

The powerful backrower has emerged as one of Navatu’s standout players in its historic Vodafone Super Deans campaign.

His game is built around physicality and aggression.

He thrives in collisions, enjoys the hard work of clearing and contesting rucks and brings an intensity that has made him a constant presence in the forward pack.

But Kanawabu is not simply a player who relies on brute strength.

His deceptive pace and decent footwork allow him to become a threat in open play, giving Navatu another attacking option when the game breaks up.

For head coach Alipate Ravulo, Kanawabu’s development has been a journey that began long before he arrived at Navatu. Ravulo coached him at club level and took him around the Northern Division to compete in Sevens tournaments, giving the youngster valuable exposure and helping shape his rugby career.

“I have nurtured him from club games and taken him around the Northern Division to play sevens,” Ravulo said.

Ravulo believes Kanawabu has returned from the national age-grade environment with valuable knowledge that has benefited the entire Navatu squad.

“He has shared his knowledge and experience with his fellow Northern brothers on what he went through in the rugby pathway,” Ravulo said.

Kanawabu, meanwhile, remains grateful for the opportunity to return to the Northern schools rugby scene with Navatu and be part of a team that has rewritten the school’s history.

“It has enabled me to be part of the historic rise of the school in the competition.”

item.title: Team Fiji Athletes honoured
item.description: TEAM Fiji’s Glasgow 2026 campaign was celebrated last Saturday as athletes were formally recognised at a thanksgiving dinner at the Holiday Inn, Suva. Commonwealth Games gold medallist Taniela Rainibogi and boxing’s brinze medallist Jasmine Daunakamakama received their reward cheques from Minister for Youth and Sports Jese Saukuru at the Holiday Inn.
item.content:encoded:
TEAM Fiji’s Glasgow 2026 campaign was celebrated last Saturday as athletes were formally recognised at a thanksgiving dinner at the Holiday Inn, Suva.

Commonwealth Games gold medallist Taniela Rainibogi and boxing’s brinze medallist Jasmine Daunakamakama received their reward cheques from Minister for Youth and Sports Jese Saukuru at the Holiday Inn.

Rainibogi was presented with a $15,000 cheque following his gold-medal performance in weightlifting, while Daunakamakama received $5000 after making history as the first Fijian woman to win a Commonwealth Games boxing medal.

The remaining Team Fiji athletes were presented with certificates for their contribution to Fiji’s campaign.

Saukuru told the athletes the evening was an opportunity to celebrate their efforts and the pride they brought to the country.

“Today we celebrate you, our athletes,” Saukuru said.

He said the recognition marked an important milestone for Fiji and acknowledged the commitment of the athletes who represented the country on the Commonwealth stage.

“This award marks a milestone for Fiji,” he said.

The thanksgiving dinner brought together athletes, officials, families and supporters to reflect on Fiji’s campaign in Glasgow.

Rainibogi’s gold medal and Daunakamakama’s historic boxing medal were among Fiji’s standout achievements at the Games.

The event also recognised the wider Team Fiji contingent, with certificates presented to athletes for their participation and contribution.

Saukuru thanked the athletes for their commitment and for representing Fiji with pride on the Commonwealth stage.

item.title: Walker sees huge potential in Fijiana
item.description: VODAFONE Fijiana XV head coach Willie Walker believes the future of women’s rugby in Fiji is exciting, saying the country has only begun to tap into its enormous potential. Walker made the comments after the Fijiana narrowly went down 29-22 to South Africa in their second Test at Churchill Park in Lautoka last Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
VODAFONE Fijiana XV head coach Willie Walker believes the future of women’s rugby in Fiji is exciting, saying the country has only begun to tap into its enormous potential.

Walker made the comments after the Fijiana narrowly went down 29-22 to South Africa in their second Test at Churchill Park in Lautoka last Saturday.

Despite the defeat, Walker was encouraged by the fight shown by his players and believes there is plenty of room for growth as Fiji continues to develop its women’s rugby programme.

“I think from what I’ve seen in my limited time here, it’s exciting.

“This is one of the reasons why I decided to apply for this job, because there’s so much potential in this country,” Walker said.

Walker said providing players with more opportunities, education and high-performance training would be crucial to unlocking that potential.

“I don’t think we’ve even touched the surface of the potential that is actually available.”

The coach said he continues to see young boys and girls playing rugby in communities, raising the question of whether Fiji has identified all the players capable of progressing to the highest level.

“I’m still, when driving down the street, seeing boys and girls playing out in the middle of the field and I’m thinking, have we actually captured everybody? And I don’t think we have yet,” he said.

Walker said his immediate focus would be to build on the foundations laid during the Test series as the Fijiana prepare for their next challenge against Japan.

“We went back to basics, we stripped it all back to the fundamentals of rugby.

“We’ve just got to continue over the next two to three weeks to build on those aspects of the game,” he added.

Walker stressed that developing the Fijiana would be a long-term process, with conditioning, skills and decision-making among the key areas requiring attention.

“There’s a lot of work to still be done obviously, but it’s an exciting opportunity to do that,” he said.

As the team looks towards Japan, Walker said the focus would be on improving the smaller details rather than attempting to make drastic changes.

“We’re not trying to do things that are outside of our reach. We want to stay within what we can do and what we’re capable of.

“We just have to be more accurate around some of the decision-making and then the skill-set stuff.”
